title: The Way to School
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: How do students get to school? The answer depends on where they live, how far they must travel and what services are available, and it has important consequences for health, for traffic and for the environment. In the imaginary country of Altonia, the Ministry of Education surveyed students in four very different towns to find out how they travel, and published the results as pie charts. The towns were chosen to represent four types of community: a mountain village, a big city, an island and a farming district. This passage describes the findings and considers what other countries can learn from them.

In the mountain village, half of the students walk to school and the other half go by school bus. The village is small, so many children live within a kilometre of the school, and the steep roads make cycling difficult. Those who live higher up the valley, however, would have to walk for more than an hour, and so the council provides a bus for them. Parents in the village say that the walk is one of the pleasures of the day, since the children meet their friends on the way and arrive at school awake and ready to learn, although in winter the snow can make the journey hard.

The big city offers four main choices, and students use them in almost equal numbers: a quarter walk, a quarter cycle, a quarter take the bus or metro, and a quarter travel by car. This is the result of a deliberate policy. The city has built safe cycle lanes, made public transport cheap for students and limited parking near schools, so that parents have less reason to drive. City officials say that the aim is not to ban cars but to make other choices equally attractive, and that the policy has reduced the traffic jams outside schools every morning.

On the island, the picture is very different: nine out of ten students travel by boat. Villages are separated by water, and there are almost no roads, so a ferry is the only practical way to reach the school on the neighbouring island, and the remaining tenth live close enough to walk. The boat journey takes about twenty minutes, and students use it to do their homework or to chat. The island's ferry service is expensive to run, and the Ministry pays almost the whole cost, because it believes that no child should miss an education because of the sea.

In the farming district, the figures divide into three almost equal parts. About a third of the students are driven to school by their parents, a third come on a school bus, and a third cycle along quiet country roads. Distances are long, and farms are scattered across a wide area, so no single method is suitable for everyone. The district has the highest proportion of students who arrive late, because buses are sometimes delayed by mud in the wet season, and local officials have asked the Ministry for money to pave the worst roads.

Dr Katarzyna Nowak, a health researcher who analysed the survey, observes that students who walk or cycle are more active and more alert in morning lessons than those who arrive by car. She recommends that every school should encourage active travel where distances allow, and that governments should make the routes safe. According to her calculations, a child who cycles three kilometres to school and back each day gains the equivalent of the exercise recommended for the whole day, without any additional time spent in a gym or on a sports field. She also notes that parents often drive their children only because the roads feel dangerous, and that cheap measures such as crossings, lights and traffic calming can change that feeling.

The Ministry has not yet decided what to do. It is considering a plan to pay for crossing guards and bicycle sheds in schools throughout the country, which would cost relatively little. It is also considering a scheme in which groups of parents would take turns to walk with children to school, an idea known as a walking bus. Both measures have been tried with success in other countries. The Ministry says that it will make a decision after a second survey, to be carried out in two years, which will show whether the habits of students are changing as roads and services improve.
